Introduction - February 2012 











#### **Base metals reality check?** 

Base metal prices have performed strongly in recent months. The Thomson Reuters GFMS Base Metals Index, which gives equal weight to all of the base metals, has risen from a low of 267.65 on October 20th in the final quarter of 2011 to a recent high of 322.92 on January 30th. 

Certainly, the advances seen since the start of the year have not had much support from the broader fundamentals.  In

the individual sections, we do not note any particularly significant pickup in activity in downstream fabricating markets, apart from some opportunistic buying as the late 2011/early 2012 price rally began to show surprising pace. The increase in prices has taken some pressure off the high cost producers. However, it should be remembered that despite the low prices seen in the early part of the final quarter of last year, margins were still excellent for the producers of base metals, with the notable exception of the marginal cost aluminium suppliers in China and Western Europe, and the Chinese nickel pig iron producers. Therefore, for the price momentum to be sustained, there has to be an improvement in demand, as we do not expect much support from the supply side at current price levels. In the short term, we are not expecting this improvement in demand to occur. As such, Thomson Reuters GFMS expects the correction in base metals prices, which began to emerge towards the end of January, to continue. It should be noted, however, that the average annual price for 2012 that we are forecasting for each of the base metals is above where prices reside in early February, with the exception of nickel. This fits in with our view that the price weakness will be relatively short-lived and that prices should finish the year on a firmer note. ##### **~~Difference between Thomson Reuters GFMS Price Forecast and Reuters Base Metals Poll Forecast Mean for 2012~~** 10

##### **Is a price consensus emerging?** Thomson Reuters has just published its analysts’ survey of market balance and price projections for 2012 (see chart above). For all the base metals, apart from nickel, we are slightly above the mean forecasts in the survey. For aluminium, although our forecasts are broadly in line, we are one of the few companies that is projecting a market deficit in 2012 (130,000 tonnes), compared to a mean surplus of 492,000 tonnes. This is based on the belief that production cutbacks in high cost regions will remain an issue and will limit the growth in global output to 1.4% this year. However, even our forecast of a deficit will not have any significant impact on the stock overhang. As such, the bulk of the price support for aluminium will come from the cost curve rather than the underlying fundamentals. South Korean IP during September to November averaged 6.4% growth year-on-year, but was showing gradually slower expansion over the period.  However, December saw a sharp fall in industrial output, to 2.8%; the average factory operating rate of 77.6% was the lowest since August 2009 and the ratio of inventories to shipments of finished goods was the highest since January 2009.  Having underperformed market expectations, there is growing anticipation that policymakers could implement more relief action. Meanwhile, in Taiwan, the slide in IP continued in December, falling by 8.1% year-on-year, following a 4.7% decline in November (the first fall in 28 months).  The government has said that the outlook for Taiwan’s export orders and IP remains dim for at least the first half of the year, as demand from Europe and China continue to deteriorate; US orders, though remained strong.

**A2** Aluminium - February 2012 new financial year as demand is expected to continue its post-earthquake/tsunami recovery. ##### **Chinese consumption leads 2011 global growth; Japan** ##### **and US lag** Based on data from the World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS), total global consumption of primary aluminium last year through November increased by 6.2%, to 39.14 million tonnes. Apart from Japan, all of the major consuming countries and regions exhibited positive year-on-year demand growth over the eleven months. Japanese consumption, according to the WBMS, did pick up in the second half of 2011, but for the whole eleven months was still down by 5.5% year-on-year. Data from the Japanese Aluminium Association (JAA) showed that flat rolled product output fell by 12.4% in November and was 6.2% lower year-on-year over the eleven months, at 1.106 million tonnes. Production of extrusions rose by 3.6% in November and was 2.0% higher for the year to date, at 723,000 tonnes. The JAA reported a 3.3% fall in total enduse of aluminium products in November, and over the whole eleven months this was down by 2.2%, at 3.532 million tonnes. Also reflecting the aftermath of the earthquake and tsunami, independent data show that sales of motor vehicles (cars, trucks, buses and commercial vans) in Japan fell by 15.1% in 2011 to 4.210 million, with sales of passenger cars down 16.3% to 3.525 million. The Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association (JAMA) recently forecast a 19% rise in total motor vehicle sales this year (back to 2008 levels), with passenger car sales up 22%. US demand was estimated by the WBMS to be just 0.7% higher for the year through November than for the same period in 2010. Meanwhile, the Aluminum Association (AA) net new aluminium mill order index rose by 4.6% year-onyear in December, but was 2.3% down on November. For the whole of 2011, mill orders were higher by 6.6% year-onyear. The Metals Service Cen

ter Institute (MSCI) recorded US service center shipments of aluminium products up by 5.2% in December and 15% greater for the whole of 2011. Looking ahead, Sapa is anticipating that North American extrusion demand will grow by 5-7% this year; the transport market is expected to grow by 5-10%; distribution, industrial residential building and construction and automotive by 0-5%; but the commercial building and construction market is expected to be down by 0-5%. We are carrying a slightly higher figure given that the ILZSG data is still incorporating a number of estimates and some full year production data have become available. For example, production increased at Xstrata’s two plants in Europe (San Juan de Nieva and Nordenham); in part due to the introduction of a 20,000 tpy direct leaching plant at the latter facility. The company’s total refined zinc production nevertheless fell by 4%, to 738,000 tonnes, due to the closure of Kidd Creek in Canada. Vedanta, the leading zinc producer in India, reported that output in the first nine months of last year was 10% higher at 569,000 tonnes, which is again slightly greater than suggested by the initial ILZSG data. ##### **Concentrate output growth begins to gain momentum** The key to the limited growth in refined zinc output was tightness at the concentrate stage, which importantly is beginning to be alleviated; linked to this has been the modest gain in Chinese production.
